items.title: Prompt caching se AI ka jawab badal jata hai? Aur lambi chat idle chhodo to?
items.one_idea: Prompt caching only reuses the already-processed prompt prefix and never changes the answer; Claude Code now also compacts a very long idle chat before its one-hour cache expires so your next message does not reprocess everything.
items.spoken_hook: Prompt caching se AI ka jawab badal jata hai?
items.hook_10s: AI interview mein pucha: caching se AI ka jawab badal jata hai? Nahi, jawab bilkul same rehta hai. Isme teen baatein hain. [frame 0: two identical answer bubbles joined by an equals sign]
items.visual_idea: A prompt block is stamped 'processed' and kept in a box with a ticking clock; two answer bubbles with and without the box come out identical; near the end of the clock a long chat shrinks to a short card before the box closes.
items.everyday_anchor: You wait for a lift and the same chai order is remembered by the cafe so it is made faster, but it tastes the same.
items.example: Label example: a 200K token chat idle ~54 minutes gets compacted (release note); cache read 0.1x, 5-min write 1.25x (docs).
facts_to_verify: v2.1.299 (14 Oct 2026): 200K+ token chat idle ~54 min is compacted before its one-hour cache expires
Caching has no effect on output generation; response is identical
cache read 0.1x, 5-minute write 1.25x, default 5-min lifetime
Idle compaction is stated for the terminal (Claude Code CLI) only

items.notes: Caveats: idle compaction is documented for the terminal only, do not generalize; release note says 54 min vs a one-hour cache while docs say default cache is 5 min (the 1-hour option is the one in play), explain or leave out; no savings percentage in sources, never claim one; do not say 'new' for caching itself. hook_type misconception_question is NOT yet allowed by validate_queue.py (see state/proposals/2026-10-17-misconception-question.md); validation fails on e101 until the owner approves.

items.title: Context mein kya-kya jata hai? Context ke 5 sources
items.one_idea: The context is everything the model sees when it answers: system prompt, tools, examples, message history and external data, and each source should stay lean.

items.title: Context compaction kya hai? Lambi chat ko chhota kaise karte hain
items.one_idea: Compaction summarises a conversation that is nearing the window limit and restarts a new window with the summary, while low-risk pruning drops redundant tool outputs.

items.hook_10s: Context compaction kya hota hai? Lambi chat ko summary banakar chhota karna. Teen steps. [frame 0: a full window bar shrinking to a small summary card]

facts_to_verify: compaction: summarising contents and reinitiating a new context window with the summary
low-risk pruning: discarding redundant tool outputs or messages

items.title: RAG kya hai? AI ko apni notebook dekhne do
items.one_idea: RAG retrieves relevant information from a knowledge base and adds it to the user's prompt, so the model answers from your documents.
items.spoken_hook: RAG kya hai?

items.everyday_anchor: Looking up the right page in your notes before answering an exam question.
items.example: Label example: a company handbook split into pages.
facts_to_verify: RAG pairs a pretrained language model with an external retrieval component (Lewis et al.)
RAG retrieves relevant information from a knowledge base and appends it to the user's prompt
chunks turned into embeddings; most similar retrieved at runtime

items.title: Interview: Poora PDF context mein daal doon ya RAG banaun?

facts_to_verify: under 200,000 tokens you can include the whole knowledge base in the prompt, RAG not needed

items.title: Model pichli chat kyun bhool jata hai? AI ki memory notebook
items.one_idea: The context window is a small, limited desk that gets cluttered as it fills; agent memory means writing notes to storage outside the window and reading them back when needed, and the memory tool is that notebook: a /memories folder your own app manages.
items.spoken_hook: Model pichli chat kyun bhool jata hai?
items.hook_10s: Model pichli chat kyun bhool jata hai? Kyunki uski desk chhoti hai. Notebook se yaad rakhta hai. Teen steps. [frame 0: a small desk crowded with papers beside an empty notebook]
items.visual_idea: A small desk fills with papers until it overflows; the model writes a note into a notebook shelf outside the desk, the desk is cleared, and a later question pulls the same note back onto the clean desk.
items.everyday_anchor: You note an exam formula in your copy so you can clear your desk and find it again tomorrow.

items.title: How a model learns: forward pass, loss, gradient descent
items.one_idea: A model learns by guessing, measuring how wrong the guess was (the loss) and nudging its weight against the gradient, repeated until it converges; the same loop trains an LLM.
items.spoken_hook: AI model seekhta kaise hai?
items.hook_source: the owner's own wording of 2026-10-19: the plain question, a 0.6 s pause, then the basketball analogy as the first teaching line (the filler 'kya use ratwaya jaata hai? Bilkul nahi!' between the hook and the start was cut by the owner)
items.visual_idea: A ball and hoop with four marks (shot, miss, understand, try again), then three cards hours to marks with one weight dial, a loss gauge, a loss curve with a dot sliding against the gradient arrow and a table of real runs, then the same run diverging with a larger step.
items.everyday_anchor: Learning basketball: take a shot, miss, understand the mistake, try again.
items.example: EXAMPLE (we ran it, Python 3.12): one weight w, marks = w x hours for 1, 2, 3 hours giving 2, 4, 6. Learning rate 0.1: w 1.867 and loss 0.083 after one update, w 2.0 after four. Learning rate 0.5: loss 18.667, 250.963, 3374.058 (diverges). Check question: marks 3, 6, 9 give w = 3.

items.title: Train, validation and test: three piles of data
items.one_idea: Data is split into three piles with three jobs: the model learns from train, validation is how we choose between models, and the test pile is opened once at the end, because only data the model has never seen says how it will do on new data.
items.spoken_hook: Train, validation aur test data alag kyun rakhte hain?
items.hook_source: the plain direct question (9 words), then the exam analogy as the first teaching line, no filler in between (owner's rule 8 of 2026-10-19)
items.visual_idea: A textbook, a mock test and a final exam become three piles; a grid of 1,000 dots is cut into three blocks of true size (70, 15, 15 percent); a model that memorises scores 100 on train and 72 on validation; a second model scores 82 on both and wins on validation; the test pile opens once and shows 79; peeking at the test score and changing the model turns the green pile gold.
items.everyday_anchor: Exam preparation: textbook practice, a mock test, then a final exam with questions you have never seen.
items.example: EXAMPLE (we ran it, Python 3.12 and numpy, seed 36, 1,000 fake points, 700 train, 150 validation, 150 test): model 1 copies the closest training point: train 100 percent, validation 72, test 71. Model 2 averages 151 neighbours (picked by validation among 1, 5, 15, 51, 151): train 82, validation 82, test 79. Median of 200 seeds: 100, 73, 72 and 81, 81, 79. The 1,000 emails are only the story; the script says the data is fake.
facts_to_verify: Training, validation and test sets and their jobs; repeated use of the test set makes the model fit it (Google ML Crash Course, fetched 2026-10-19). A model that only repeats the labels it has seen scores perfectly and fails on new data; tuning on the test set lets knowledge of it leak into the model (scikit-learn, fetched 2026-10-19). Every accuracy on screen is from the real run printed in docs-notes/pilot-script-day2.md.

items.title: Interview: Temperature, Top-K aur Top-P ka difference batao
items.one_idea: Top-K keeps a fixed count of the most probable next words, Top-P keeps the smallest set reaching a cumulative probability threshold, and Temperature reshapes the probability distribution.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ne poocha: LLM mein Temperature, Top-K aur Top-P ka difference batao.
items.hook_source: the owner's own script of 2026-10-19, used word for word
items.visual_idea: One next-word distribution for Aaj mausam bahut is cut at three for Top-K, accumulated to 90 percent for Top-P, and reshaped from sharp to flat for Temperature; NAMKEEN marks the tail.
items.example: EXAMPLE: a toy run with invented scores for 8 words after 'Aaj mausam bahut' (state/runs/q105_toy_run.py, output in state/runs/q105_toy_run_output.txt): at T=1 ACHHA 36.7 %, GARAM 24.6 %, THANDA 16.5 %, NAMKEEN 0.6 %; top-k 3 leaves NAMKEEN out; top-p 0.9 keeps five words at T=1 and six at T=1.5; NAMKEEN is 0.015 % at T=0.5 and 1.874 % at T=1.5.
items.cover_headline: Temperature, Top-K, Top-P: what's the difference?
items.caption_note: Use the owner's command hook unchanged; one comment ask about NAMKEEN, with the answer not shown in the reel.
facts_to_verify: top_k: the number of highest probability vocabulary tokens kept for top-k filtering (Hugging Face GenerationConfig docs, fetched 2026-10-20)
top_p: only the smallest set of most probable tokens whose probabilities add up to top_p or higher are kept (same page)
temperature: the value used to modulate the next token probabilities (same page); sampling must be on (do_sample) for these to apply

items.title: Interview: Prompt mein examples dene se model hamesha behtar hota hai?
items.one_idea: Examples in a prompt show the model the shape of the answer and the allowed labels, so they usually help; but every example costs tokens on every request, a one-sided set or a bad order pulls the answer, and the only way to know is to measure with and without.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ne poocha: prompt mein examples dene se model hamesha behtar jawab deta hai?
items.hook_formula: interviewer_asked: one complete question of 11 words in plain words
items.hook_source: hook-writer interviewer_asked; the question passes the Question quality test (one sentence, 11 words, no stacked question, no jargon beyond 'prompt', 'examples', 'model')
items.visual_idea: The real classification prompt as a mono card under the hook from frame 0; it grows from 23 to 85 tokens when five examples are added (a real tiktoken count); two label chips feed a model box; three all-positive examples make a red ALWAYS POSITIVE? pill; a gauge from NEAR CHANCE to NEAR BEST swings with the examples and their order; three measuring runs (0, 3, 5 examples) on the same reviews.
items.everyday_anchor: Showing a new hire a few solved tickets before the real one: a good set teaches the format, a one-sided set teaches a bad habit.
items.example: EXAMPLE prompt (invented): 'Classify the review as positive or negative.' with up to five Review/Label pairs and the review 'The delivery was late and the box was damaged.' We ran tiktoken (o200k_base): 0 examples 23 tokens, 1 example 35, 3 examples 60, 5 examples 85; five examples add 62 tokens to every request, 62 million tokens over a million requests. No model result is shown or claimed.
facts_to_verify: Examples steer output format, tone and structure; they should be relevant and diverse so the model does not pick up unintended patterns; 3 to 5 examples (Anthropic prompting best practices, fetched 2026-10-19).

GPT-3 few-shot accuracy depends on the prompt format, the training examples and their order, from near chance to near state of the art; the model is biased toward answers near the end of the prompt or common in pre-training data (Zhao et al., 'Calibrate Before Use', abstract, fetched 2026-10-19).

Randomly replacing the labels in the demonstrations barely hurts performance across 12 models; the label space, the distribution of the input text and the overall format of the demonstrations matter (Min et al., abstract, fetched 2026-10-19).

Reasoning models often do not need few-shot examples: try zero shot first, then few shot if needed; examples must align closely with the instructions (OpenAI reasoning best practices, fetched 2026-10-19).
Token counts are from tiktoken o200k_base on the exact prompt shown; other models tokenize differently. API usage is billed per token (Anthropic pricing page, fetched 2026-10-19).
items.cover_headline: Do more examples always help?
keywords: how many examples in a prompt
items.trap: Adding examples blindly. Reframed after reading the sources: labels barely matter (Min et al.), so the trap is not 'a wrong example is copied'; it is cost on every request, a one-sided or badly ordered set that pulls the answer, and never measuring against the no-example prompt.
items.caption_note: The answer to the check question is: positive (the model may lean toward positive when all three examples are positive). Put it in the caption.

items.title: Interview: Temperature, top-k aur top-p teeno laga diye. Output pe kaun sa asar karta hai?
items.one_idea: Temperature, top-k and top-p do three different jobs: top-k (by count) and top-p (by total chance) cut the list of next words, temperature only reshapes the chances of the words that are left, and changing one changes what another keeps.
items.spoken_hook: Chatbot ne bola: aaj mausam bahut namkin hai.
items.hook_source: the stake from frame 0 (the bot says something silly), then the interview question, then the answer first in one plain sentence (owner's rule 8 and his correction of 2026-10-19: no filler between the hook and the answer)
items.visual_idea: A chat where the bot says the weather is salty, then one toy list of 8 candidate words drawn as bars with their real chances (NAMKIN 0.6 percent); temperature 1.5 flattens the bars and makes NAMKIN three times likelier without removing it; a cut line after word 3 (top-k) removes it; a running total stops at 90 percent after 5 words (top-p); the same top-p keeps 6 words once the bars are flatter.
items.everyday_anchor: Choosing the next word like picking from a menu: top-k and top-p shorten the menu, temperature changes how strongly the menu favours the first items.
items.example: EXAMPLE (we ran it, Python 3.12 and numpy, invented logits for 8 words after 'Aaj mausam bahut ...'): at T 1.0 ACHHA 36.7 percent and NAMKIN 0.6 percent; T 1.5 makes NAMKIN 1.9 percent (3.1 times) and removes nothing; top-k 3 keeps ACHHA, GARAM, THANDA (47.2, 31.6, 21.2 after renormalising) and NAMKIN is never drawn in 10,000 draws; top-p 0.9 adds 36.7, 61.4, 77.9, 88.9, 95.0 and keeps 5 words; T 0.5 gives ACHHA 56.3 percent, T 1.5 gives 28.8; top-p 0.9 keeps 5 words at T 1.0 and 6 words at T 1.5. Order of the stack in the run: temperature, then top-k, then top-p, then renormalise.
facts_to_verify: Anthropic Messages API reference (fetched 2026-10-19): temperature is the amount of randomness injected into the response (default 1.0, range 0.0 to 1.0, closer to 0.0 for analytical tasks, closer to 1.0 for creative ones, not fully deterministic even at 0.0); top_k samples only from the top K options for each token to remove the long tail; top_p uses nucleus sampling: cumulative distribution in decreasing probability order, cut off once it reaches top_p. The same page marks all three as not settable on models released after Claude Opus 4.6 (not used in the reel).

Hugging Face 'How to generate text' (fetched 2026-10-19): lower temperature makes the softmax sharper; top-k keeps the K most likely next words and redistributes the probability mass among them; top-p picks from the smallest set of words whose cumulative probability exceeds p, so the set size changes with the distribution; top-p can be combined with top-k.

Holtzman et al., nucleus sampling (arXiv 1904.09751, fetched 2026-10-19): sampling from the dynamic nucleus of the distribution cuts the unreliable tail and avoids bland, repetitive likelihood-based text.

Every number on screen is from the seeded toy run in docs: toy_run.py (invented logits, labelled EXAMPLE); the claim 'top-p keeps more words when temperature is higher' is a result of that run and follows from flatter chances needing more words to reach p.
items.cover_headline: Temperature, top-k, top-p: who does what?
items.caption_note: The answer to the check question is: badhte hain (put it in the caption).

items.title: Overfitting: zero error on training, 133 on new data
items.one_idea: A flexible model can score zero error on its training points and still fail on new data because it memorised the noise; unseen data exposes it, and simpler models, more data and validation fix it, while a too-simple model underfits.
items.spoken_hook: Ek AI model ka training error zero hai, phir bhi naye questions par uski galti 133 hai!
items.visual_idea: Training Error 0.00 vs New Data Error 133 on frame 0; exam-student analogy; a 10-point scatter with a straight line (0.87 / 1.04) and a wiggly curve through all points (0 / 133); the curve with 100 points (0.93 / 1.03); a straight line missing a curved pattern for underfitting.
items.everyday_anchor: The student who memorises solved examples and fails when the question changes.
items.example: EXAMPLE from the owner's own Python run: hidden rule y = 2x + 1 plus random noise, 10 training points; straight line train 0.87, new data 1.04; flexible curve train 0 and new data 133, actual y roughly 1 to 21; same curve with 100 points train 0.93, new data 1.03. The studio must re-run this (a script in state/runs) and show the real printed numbers; if they differ from the owner's, report it and do not change the script yourself.
facts_to_verify: Overfitting = low training error, high error on new data; underfitting = model too simple (scikit-learn example page, to be fetched by the researcher/studio). Every number on screen comes from the printed run.
items.cover_headline: Zero training error, still wrong?

items.title: Interview: Chain-of-thought prompting hamesha performance badhata hai?
items.one_idea: Chain-of-thought (step by step) prompting helps on multi-step problems, but on simple questions it only adds output tokens, latency and cost, and reasoning models already reason internally, so test both on your own examples.
items.spoken_hook: France ki capital poochhi… Bot ne teen lines mein jawab diya!
items.hook_formula: bot over-explains a one-word answer, then the interview question
items.visual_idea: Chat that answers 'capital of France' in three lines vs one word; shop bill with 3 notebooks at 45, 2 pens at 12, paid 200: 135 + 24 = 159, change 41; Standard LLM vs Reasoning model; the interview answer card.
items.everyday_anchor: A shop bill: writing the steps catches a calculation slip, but nobody needs steps to say Paris.
items.example: EXAMPLE (invented, arithmetic checked: 3 x 45 = 135, 2 x 12 = 24, total 159, change 200 - 159 = 41). No model result is shown or claimed.
facts_to_verify: Chain-of-thought prompting (intermediate reasoning steps) improves arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning mainly in sufficiently large models (Wei et al., abstract, fetched 2026-10-20).
items.cover_headline: Does step by step always help?
items.trap: Adding 'think step by step' to every prompt without measuring.
items.caption_note: Comment ALWAYS or TEST FIRST; the answer is TEST FIRST (put it in the caption).
items.studio_note: OWNER'S OWN SCRIPT, approved with his edits on 2026-10-20 and re-formatted only (Devanagari for Hindi words, Roman for English, {spoken} forms for numbers). Keep every line; do not rewrite or shorten. Voice: make_voice picks the owner's voice.

items.title: Interview: Developer aur user instruction mein takraav ho to AI kiski maane?
items.one_idea: Developer instructions take precedence over conflicting user instructions, but a prompt is not a security boundary, so critical business rules such as a refund limit must be enforced in trusted backend code.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: Developer की instruction और user के message में टकराव हो, तो AI किसका order follow करेगा?
items.hook_formula: interviewer_asked (owner's wording; question runs longer than 16 words)
items.visual_idea: Interviewer question card; refund bot with a 500 rupee limit and a customer asking for 2,000; chain of command System > Developer > User; a code run where the model returns Approved and the backend prints Approved: False.
items.everyday_anchor: A refund bot with a 500 rupee limit that a customer tries to talk past.
items.example: EXAMPLE (invented): refund limit 500, request 2,000, model stub always says yes, backend check prints Approved: False. The studio runs a few lines of Python and shows the real output.
facts_to_verify: OpenAI Model Spec chain of command (fetched 2026-10-20): when developer and user messages conflict, the developer messages have greater authority. The script says 'System instructions' in the owner's own wording; the spec's own name for the top level is 'platform'. Keep the owner's word in the script and voice and report the difference, do not change it.
items.cover_headline: Developer or user: who wins?
items.trap: Writing a business rule only in the prompt and trusting it.
items.caption_note: Comment PROMPT or CODE; the answer is CODE (put it in the caption).

items.title: An LLM is a next-word predictor: watch the guesses
items.one_idea: An LLM writes by repeatedly making a list of possible next words with odds, picking one and adding it; the answer is built one word at a time.
items.spoken_hook: ChatGPT jawab kaise likhta hai? Ek ek word guess karke!
items.visual_idea: The sentence 'the cat sat on the' with a ranked bar list of next-word guesses (mat 50 %, sofa 33 %, bed 17 %); the picked word is appended and the list rebuilds; a phone keyboard suggestion strip as the anchor; a label TOKEN = word piece.
items.everyday_anchor: The phone keyboard's next-word suggestions.
items.example: EXAMPLE (toy counting model on an invented 8-sentence corpus, not a real LLM), real printed run state/runs/a004_next_word_run.py: after 'sat on the' seen 6 times: mat 3/6 = 50 %, sofa 2/6 = 33 %, bed 1/6 = 17 %. A real LLM does the same with a neural network over tokens; Google's crash course says LLMs assign probabilities to continuations and a token can be a word, subword or character.
facts_to_verify: LLMs predict tokens and assign probabilities to continuations; a token can be a word, a subword or a single character (Google ML crash course, fetched 2026-10-21).
items.cover_headline: How ChatGPT really writes
items.caption_note: Comment question: agar hamesha top guess chune, to jawab har baar same aayega? (answer in caption)

items.title: Interview: Model ne confidently galat fact bol diya. Hallucination kyun hoti hai, aur kaise kam karoge?
items.one_idea: A model predicts likely next words and does not look facts up, and training and benchmark grading that reward guessing over saying 'I don't know' make it answer confidently anyway; you reduce it by grounding answers in retrieved sources (RAG), allowing 'I don't know', and checking outputs.
items.spoken_hook: Chatbot ने fake research paper बताया, बिल्कुल confidently!
items.hook_formula: chatbot confidently wrong, then the interview question
items.visual_idea: Chat showing a confident answer with a made-up paper title; five candidate answers with odds and the top pick wrong 70 % of the time; grading table (right +1, wrong 0 or -1, I don't know 0) flipping guess to abstain; RAG: question + retrieved page -> answer; the interview answer card.
items.everyday_anchor: An exam where a blank answer scores 0 and a wrong answer also scores 0: you always guess.
items.example: EXAMPLE (invented odds), real run state/runs/q110_halluc_run.py: top guess A at 30 % is wrong 70 % of the time; with right +1 / wrong 0 / blank 0 expected score of guessing 0.30 vs 0.00, with wrong -1 it is -0.40, so abstain.
items.cover_headline: Why does AI make up facts?
items.trap: Calling it a bug to patch: the model predicts likely words, it does not look facts up.
items.caption_note: Comment question: blank answer ko 0 marks do ya galat ko minus? (put the answer in the caption)
facts_to_verify: arXiv 2509.04664: training and benchmark grading reward guessing over saying 'I don't know' (abstract); arXiv 2005.11401: RAG, retrieval-augmented generation (abstract). Fetched in the planning session of 2026-10-21.

items.title: Interview: Open source model use karoge ya closed API? Decide kaise karoge?
items.one_idea: Decide on data privacy and control, cost at your own request volume (an API is pay per use, self-hosting is a fixed server bill plus someone to run it) and the licence terms, not on benchmark scores alone; start with an API and move when volume or privacy demands it.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: Open source model use करोगे या closed API, ये decide कैसे करोगे?
items.visual_idea: Two doors OPEN MODEL (you run it) and API (they run it); a break-even line chart of monthly cost (API rising line vs flat server bill crossing at 120,000 requests); a licence card with 'Built with Meta Llama 3' and the 700 million users clause; Apache 2.0 card; the interview answer card.
items.everyday_anchor: Taxi vs buying a car.
items.example: EXAMPLE (invented prices), real run state/runs/q111_cost_run.py: API Rs 0.5 per request vs GPU server Rs 60,000 per month fixed: 20,000 requests Rs 10,000 vs 60,000; 120,000 requests Rs 60,000 vs 60,000 (break-even); 500,000 requests Rs 250,000 vs 60,000.
items.cover_headline: Open model or paid API?
items.trap: Picking on benchmark scores alone instead of data privacy, cost at your volume and who runs it.
items.caption_note: Comment API or OPEN: 20,000 requests a month, which one? (answer API, in the caption)
facts_to_verify: Llama 3 licence 700 million monthly active users clause; Apache 2.0 allows commercial use; OpenAI API data not used for training by default, abuse logs up to 30 days (pages listed in sources, fetched 2026-10-21).

items.title: Pretraining: how an LLM first learns language from text
items.one_idea: Pretraining is training a model from scratch on a huge pile of raw text with one task, guess the next word; nobody labels anything, the text itself is the answer sheet, and the error falls as it reads more.
items.spoken_hook: ChatGPT ने language कैसे सीखी? बहुत सारा text पढ़कर!
items.visual_idea: A sentence 'the dog sat on the ___' with the last word hidden; the model's guess bars, then the hidden word revealed and the error shown as one number; a loss line falling from 3.58 to 2.19 as the text pile grows (10, 20, 40, 53 words); a pile of books labelled RAW TEXT, no labels; a label PRETRAINED = raw text predictor.
items.everyday_anchor: Fill-in-the-blank practice: a student who has read a lot of text gets better at guessing the missing word, with the answer printed on the next line.
items.example: EXAMPLE (toy counting model on an invented 53-word corpus with 12 distinct words, not a real LLM), real run state/runs/a005_pretrain_run.py: loss before reading 3.58 bits per word (even guess among 12 words); after 10 words 3.09; 20 words 2.74; 40 words 2.37; all 53 words 2.19. A real LLM does the same job with a neural network over tokens and trillions of words.
facts_to_verify: Hugging Face LLM course (fetched 2026-10-22): 'Pretraining is the act of training a model from scratch: the weights are randomly initialized' and the training starts without any prior knowledge; trained on large amounts of raw text in a self-supervised fashion; next-word prediction (from the n previous words) is given as an example objective. Fine-tuning is the training done after pretraining, supervised, on human-annotated labels. Do not say 'trillions of words' or name any real model's data size in the reel: not verified.
items.cover_headline: How an LLM first learns language
items.caption_note: Comment question: pretraining mein text ko labels kisne diye? (answer: kisi ne nahi, agla word hi answer hai; put it in the caption)

items.title: Interview: Embeddings ko compare karne ke liye cosine similarity kyun, seedhi distance kyun nahi?
items.one_idea: Cosine similarity compares the direction of two embedding vectors (what they are about) and ignores their length, while plain distance also punishes a difference in length; when every vector is scaled to length 1 (as OpenAI's embeddings already are) the two give the same ranking.
items.spoken_hook: Refund search किया, cricket का note ऊपर आ गया!
items.hook_formula: search picks the wrong note by distance, then the interview question
items.visual_idea: Frame 0: a search box 'refund payment' with three notes ranked by plain distance: cricket note ahead of the long refund note. Then arrows from the origin for the query, the short note, the 5x long note (same direction, longer) and the cricket note (different direction); an angle drawn between arrows; distance vs cosine table from the run; arrows squashed to length 1 and the ranking fixed; the interview answer card.
items.everyday_anchor: Two people pointing the same way, one standing close, one far away: the direction is the same.
items.example: EXAMPLE (invented word counts [refund, payment, cricket]), real run state/runs/q112_cosine_run.py: query [1,1,0]; short refund note [1,1,0] distance 0.00 cosine 1.00; same note repeated 5 times [5,5,0] distance 5.66 cosine 1.00; cricket note [0,0,1] distance 1.73 cosine 0.00. After scaling all to length 1: distance 0.00, 0.00 and 1.41, cosine unchanged.
facts_to_verify: OpenAI embeddings FAQ (fetched 2026-10-22): 'OpenAI embeddings are normalized to length 1', so cosine similarity can be computed slightly faster with a dot product and cosine similarity and Euclidean distance give identical rankings.

Google ML course (fetched 2026-10-22): cosine similarity focuses solely on the angle between vectors; the dot product is proportional to vector length; with lengths normalized to 1 the three measures are equivalent.
items.cover_headline: Cosine or distance for embeddings?
items.trap: Comparing vector lengths when only direction carries meaning.
items.caption_note: Comment 1 or 2: the 5x longer refund note, is it the same topic? (answer: yes, in the caption)
items.studio_note: The interview question must be spoken in full in the reel (owner correction 2026-10-21): Interviewer ने पूछा, embeddings compare करने के लिए cosine similarity क्यों, seedhi distance क्यों नहीं? Boundary: if vectors are already length 1 the ranking is identical, so either works (OpenAI); length matters only when it carries meaning (Google: dot product, popularity). Close to published course reel r07 (cosine similarity, 2026-10-12): keep a different picture (arrows from the origin and the distance trap, not the angle only).

items.title: Interview: Vector database ki zaroorat kab nahi padti?
items.one_idea: Searching every stored vector (exact search) is simple and perfectly accurate, and a few thousand to some hundred thousand vectors are searched in milliseconds in memory, so a vector database or approximate index is needed only when the data, speed or number of users outgrow that; approximate indexes trade some recall for speed.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: किस project में vector database की ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ती?
items.visual_idea: A shelf of 5,000 note cards searched by a hand scanning each card in 0.3 ms (real run); a growing bar of vectors 5,000 / 100,000 / 1,000,000 with memory in MB and search time in ms; two doors EXACT SCAN vs INDEX with a recall tag; the interview answer card.
items.everyday_anchor: Finding a name in a 50-page notebook by reading every page versus building an index for a library.
items.example: EXAMPLE (random vectors, 384 dimensions, float32; times are from the run machine and will differ), real run state/runs/q113_search_run.py: 5,000 vectors 8 MB, exact top-3 search 0.3 ms; 100,000 vectors 154 MB, 7.7 ms; 1,000,000 vectors 1,536 MB, 84.6 ms.
facts_to_verify: pgvector README (fetched 2026-10-22): by default exact nearest neighbor search with perfect recall; adding an index gives approximate search that trades some recall for speed.

FAISS wiki (fetched 2026-10-22): IndexFlatL2 / IndexFlatIP are exact brute-force search (all vectors compared with the query); IVF and HNSW indexes are non-exhaustive and lose the guarantee to find the nearest neighbour. Where the boundary sits (about a million vectors) is our own run, not a source: say 'typically' and 'on this run'.
items.cover_headline: Do you need a vector database?
items.trap: Reaching for a vector database for a few thousand chunks that fit in memory.
items.caption_note: Comment YES or NO: 5,000 chunks, do you need a vector database? (answer NO, in the caption)
items.studio_note: Question spoken in full is the hook itself. Close to published course reel r09 (vector databases, 2026-10-12): this one is the opposite angle (when NOT to), keep a different picture.
